tracks.title: The question every engine inherits
tracks.text: Lesson 09 point 8 — backends. This one is a sub-lesson, under the VFS. The VFS lesson ended with a clean handoff — put the catalog in the file, and the warehouse behind the Nexus. But the moment you stand an engine up… you inherit the oldest question in infrastructure. Where do the bytes actually live… and what happens when you outgrow your first answer? [curious] Every platform makes you choose a storage stack on day one… and then punishes you for changing your mind. A migration. A fork in the code. A vendor's SDK threaded through every call. And the scarier version arrives the day you go multi-tenant — does moving to a shared bucket quietly widen who can read what? This page is about a runtime that refused to answer the question. The code never chose a backend… so you can choose any of them.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A backend is a storage provider, sitting behind one of the runtime's two seams — the blob seam for large opaque files… or the structured seam for small queryable rows — selected entirely by config. The runtime code is identical across every deployment. Only the env changes. And the load-bearing idea is those two data classes. First… blobs. Large, opaque, content-addressed — tenant repos, bundles, signed artifacts, VFS files. Those go to an object store or a volume. Second… structured data. Small, relational, queried — variables, agent memory, telemetry, the registries. That goes to Postgres or SQLite. Keeping them apart is the point. You can put blobs on R2 and rows on Railway… or both on a Fly volume… and the runtime doesn't notice.

tracks.title: One screen of config
tracks.text: One screen of config. The entire storage posture of a deployment is one file — and its header states the contract in a single sentence. The runtime code is identical across every deployment… only this config changes. Let me read it to you. At the top, identity — a signing key that sits behind the deployment's identity, and a primary tenant. Then the blob section — WB underscore STORAGE, set to local, or s3, or r2… one word picks the adapter. WB underscore DATA, the path where local blobs live. And the S3 endpoint, bucket, key, and secret for the cloud case. Then the structured section — a single line, WB underscore DATABASE underscore URL. Set it… you get Postgres. Leave it unset… you get SQLite. And last, embeddings — WB underscore EMBED, which decides how text becomes a vector. [curious] Read that file top to bottom… and you've read the whole storage design. One word swaps the blob backend. The presence of a database URL swaps the structured one. And the embed knob is deliberately separate — it's how text becomes a vector, not where the vectors live. Two orthogonal axes… no hidden third one.

tracks.title: Two seams, four verbs
tracks.text: Next — two seams, four verbs. Underneath the config are two tiny interfaces… and their smallness is the whole trick. The blob seam is a behaviour with exactly four callbacks — put… get… list… and delete — and every one of them takes tenant as its first argument. The structured seam is a single handle you open and run statements against. That's the entire surface a backend has to satisfy. And adapter selection is not a framework, or a registry, or a plugin system. It is a five-line case statement on one environment variable. Picture it. When the storage variable is s3… use the S3 module. When it's r2… use the S3 module — yes, the same one. Otherwise… use the Local module. [curious] Adding a provider is one module plus one config line. Never a fork. Picture the flow as a graph. Runtime code on the left, wanting to store a bundle or query a variable. It reaches one of two seams — Storage, or DB. Each seam reaches a single decision diamond — the storage variable, or the database URL. And from each diamond, two arrows. Local files… or one S3-slash-R2 module. SQLite file… or a Postgres URL. That's the whole switch. Code hits a seam… the seam hits a case… the case names a module… and the bytes land wherever that module puts them.

tracks.title: Isolation lives above the backend
tracks.text: Now the most important idea on the page — isolation lives above the backend. Here is the claim that makes swapping backends safe… rather than terrifying. Tenant is the first argument of every storage call and every database call — by construction. There is no code path in which the backend decides who sees what. Swapping a Fly volume for R2 cannot widen access… because access was never the backend's job. [excited] Backends are interchangeable precisely because they were never trusted with security. Picture the flow. A request comes in — a token, verified. From it… the tenant, which is the organization id. That tenant becomes the first argument of every call. The seam runs put, get, list, or delete… and before any adapter touches anything, a small function strips out dot-dot and stray slashes, so a hostile key can never climb out of its prefix. From the seam… two real arrows. Local, writing under slash data, slash tenant, slash blobs. Or S3, writing the same tenant-slash-blobs key into a bucket. And there's a third path drawn on the graph… leading to a box that says backend decides access — but the arrow to it is crossed out, labelled… no such code path. [curious] Now, honesty about the test evidence. The blob seam itself is enforced by construction, not proven by a cross-tenant test — its one test is a single-tenant store, fetch, install round-trip, and there is no end-to-end cross-tenant denial test on the blob adapters today. The denial holds because tenant is the first argument of every call and the key sanitizer runs before any adapter… but that's the shape of the code, not a green test. A separate seam does carry a named cross-tenant test — the brokered key value store, a guest-facing table on SQLite, distinct from this blob seam. Its case the suite names in capital letters — TENANT ISOLATION… a tenant cannot read or overwrite another's keys. Alice and Bob store the same key name with different values. The scoped listing keeps them apart. A cross-tenant read is denied. That proves the broker's isolation, not the blob adapters' — they share the tenant-first shape, but only one is covered end to end. A confused agent… or a hostile one… lands in its own prefix… or nowhere at all.

tracks.title: One adapter, every bucket
tracks.text: Next — one adapter, every bucket. This is a depth rung… skippable if you just want the shape. The Local adapter is about forty-five lines. Blobs live under WB-DATA, slash tenant, slash blobs, slash key… and the implementation is plain file write, file read, file remove, and a wildcard for listing. The simplest durable deploy on earth is this adapter with the data path mounted on a Fly volume — persistent across redeploys, zero code change. The volume is the storage. The S3 adapter is the surprising one… because it's only one module, and it serves both Amazon S3 and Cloudflare R2. R2 is S3-compatible, so the difference is purely config. And the signing — Amazon's SigV4 — is hand-rolled on Erlang's own crypto and HTTP libraries… which means it ships with no new dependency at all. [excited] The signing function is deliberately left public, so a known test vector could verify it — the hook is there, though no such vector test is in the suite yet. Let me give you the comparison as a sentence, because a table doesn't read aloud. Local writes a file on disk. S3 writes an object to a bucket, at an Amazon endpoint, in region us-east-1. R2 writes an object too — same module — just a Cloudflare endpoint and region auto. The verdict… the only thing distinguishing the two cloud cases is two lines of config. And the same tenant-slash-blobs-slash-key shape names the file on disk and the object in the bucket… so the scope you reason about never changes when the destination does.

tracks.title: Postgres is just a URL
tracks.text: Postgres is just a URL. The structured seam flips on one question — is the database URL set, and non-empty? If so… Postgres. If not… SQLite, with files living under the data path in an underscore-db folder. And the reason any Postgres provider works is that it's just a connection URL. CrunchyData… Fly Postgres… Railway… Neon… Supabase — all indistinguishable to the runtime. One code path… no per-provider branches. Now the elegant part — the entire dialect bridge between the two backends is one regular expression. Stores write portable SQL with question-mark-one, question-mark-two placeholders. For Postgres, a small helper rewrites them to dollar-one, dollar-two. Same numbers… different sigil. And rows come back as lists either way, so the store code is identical regardless of backend. Picture the exchange as a short conversation. A store hands the database seam a query full of question-mark placeholders. If the URL is set… the seam rewrites the sigils, opens Postgres, turns SSL on, and runs it. If the URL is unset… it runs the statement untouched against a local SQLite file. And either way… rows come back, as lists. [curious] The store never learns which backend answered. Which is exactly why moving from a file to Neon is a config change… not a rewrite.

tracks.title: The flip you get for free
tracks.text: Next — the flip you get for free. Setting that database URL doesn't only move tables. It flips semantic search from brute-force… to ANN. On SQLite, the vector module stores vectors as JSON text and computes cosine similarity in Elixir, scanning every row — order n per query. That's the live-tested default… and it's genuinely fine for one library's worth of vectors. On Postgres, the engine creates the vector extension on first open, stores a real vector column, and ranks inside the database with pgvector's distance operator and an order-by-limit. Same interface either way… callers never branch. And here's what's elegant — the linear cost is made visible, not hidden. Once a brute-force search crosses twenty-five thousand vectors, the engine logs a one-time warning. Let me read it. Brute-force search over thirty-one thousand vectors on SQLite, order n per query. For sub-linear search at scale, set the database URL to get pgvector. A work pool would only buy you a constant factor — the number of cores — so the real fix at scale is sub-linear search… and the warning says so. Picture the branch as a graph. A search call at the top. A decision — are we on Postgres? If no… SQLite loads every row and ranks in Elixir, and warns past twenty-five thousand. If yes… Postgres orders by the distance operator and limits, ranked in the database, sub-linear. [excited] And the flip itself is anticlimactic. Same search call. The operator's entire migration… was one URL. One last separation — where the vectors live is this knob. How text becomes a vector is the separate embed knob. Two orthogonal axes. The embedding side is the vectors lesson's subject… not this page's.

tracks.title: Three real postures
tracks.text: Three real postures. Abstraction earns its keep when it collapses to a few concrete choices. There are three… and each one is just a few literal lines of env — the same runtime image in all three. First… single box. Storage set to local, data on a volume. Mount a Fly volume… and you're durable across redeploys, zero dependencies. You move on when your blobs need off-box durability. Second… durable blobs. Storage set to r2, with the endpoint, bucket, key, and secret — two lines different from S3. Blobs now sit on object storage… rows still on SQLite. You move on when the vector warning fires at twenty-five thousand. Third… scale. Add the database URL — point it at any Postgres, like Neon. Postgres rows… and pgvector ANN comes along for free. That's the top of the ladder. [curious] And the honest read… most single-box deploys never leave posture one, and shouldn't. SQLite on a volume is the right answer for the great majority of deployments. You climb the ladder when a specific need shows up… and each rung is additive config… not a migration.

tracks.title: The knob that isn't storage
tracks.text: The knob that isn't storage — another depth rung, skippable. One knob in that file isn't about bytes at all. The signing key is a thirty-two-byte seed, base sixty-four encoded… and it sits behind the deployment's identity. Without it, that identity regenerates on every deploy — and the moment it changes, every signature made under the old one stops verifying, and sealed ledgers no longer check out. [sighs] So it has to survive redeploys. Generating it is a one-liner with Elixir's crypto library. And like every value in this file, it lives in the platform's secret store — set with something like fly secrets set — never baked into the image. That's the rule the whole file follows. The image is byte-identical everywhere… and the things that differ between deployments are secrets… not source.

tracks.title: Where the seam ends today
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the seam ends today. The structured seam is migrating incrementally, and the code says so. Today, only the vectors store opens through the database seam — it's the sole call site. The other structured stores — variables, library, lifecycle, telemetry, the registries — still ride SQLite directly… until each is migrated. The deploy doc's own status is candid. The seam, both blob adapters, the bring-your-own-Postgres path, and signing-key persistence — built and tested. What remains… migrating each structured store onto the seam incrementally, plus a live cloud round-trip once operator credentials exist. So calibrate. The blob side, with hand-rolled signing, has a single-tenant store, fetch, install round-trip test — its cross-tenant denial and the signing are enforced by construction and left verifiable, but neither has a dedicated test yet. The named cross-tenant test belongs to the separate brokered key value store, not these blob adapters. The SQLite vector path is the live-tested default. The pgvector path is shape-tested… with the live round-trip pending real credentials. And two hardening items are noted but not yet built — per-tenant at-rest encryption, and a microVM boundary for compute isolation. [curious] And the anti-hype, said plainly. This page is not an argument to run Postgres. It's an argument that picking the default doesn't lock you in. SQLite plus a volume is genuinely the right answer for most single-box deploys… and the runtime will tell you the one moment it isn't.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I need Postgres? No — and the runtime tells you when you might. SQLite on a volume is the default, and fine for most. The one signal to flip the database URL is that logged warning at twenty-five thousand vectors. Is R2 different from S3? Not to the runtime. R2 is S3-compatible, so a single adapter serves both — r2 resolves to the exact same module as s3. The difference is two config lines. Can a tenant read another tenant's bucket prefix? No — by construction. The seam scopes every call above the backend, and the key sanitizer strips dot-dot. The blob adapters have no dedicated cross-tenant test yet, but the brokered key value store — a separate seam — does carry a named one where Alice cannot read Bob's key. Does swapping backends migrate my data? No — the seam swaps the destination, not the contents. New writes go to the new backend… moving existing bytes is a separate operation. Where does the embedding model live? When the embed knob is local, the matrix is about thirty megabytes, downloaded once into a models folder and reused. [chuckles] And what about keeping the live disk in sync? That's Litestream… same s3 trick — same command, the only difference is the URL. That's the sync lesson's home.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's backends. Not a new construct… a refusal. The runtime never chose a backend, so you can choose any — by config, never by fork. Two tiny seams… four blob verbs and one database handle… and isolation that lives above them both, so a swap can never widen access. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under the VFS — lesson nine — the disk this page gave a warehouse to. Go back there for the catalog… and come here for the floor it stands on.
